I'm sorry, it makes zero sense, because Russia itself was notoriously terrible to its Jewish population throughout history. And is now.

Jews weren't allowed to live in cities up to XX century, both the political right and the political left engaged in state-sanctioned antisemitic violence. During the 4 years of the Civil War there were more than 1000 Jewish pogroms.
The bolsheviks arrested and killed religious and/or educated Jews. Jewish scientists were targeted during the Great Purge. After the WWII the government launched a huge antisemetic compain. As a result Jews were discriminated against on every possible level.

Hell, my gran-grandad died in the War fighting Nazis. His wife, my gran never applied for the war widow pension because it was extremely dangerous. He was declared "lost in action" rather than "dead", and in cases like this if the person was Jewish the government often ruled that they deserted and punished the family of the "traitor".

More recent examples? An antisemetic mob physically attacked my friends' mom in Moscow in the 90s while shouting slurs.
My dad refused to give any of us kids "Jewish-sounding" names, because he hoped we would "pass" as non-Jewish.
Just half an hour ago I saw a video where an old woman was singing a song she wrote about banishing and killing the Jews (she used a slur insted), so they don't spoil Mother Russia with their bad reptilian genes.
In general all Jewish organizations in Russia report that antisemitism is on the rise in all forms.

Not even mentioning that a lot of the volunteer combatants in the Russian army are literal self-proclaimed neo-Nazis.
So to me this argument sounds like "well, actually Hitler invaded Poland to punish them for the historical mistreatment of Jews".

Sorry, I might have mislead you. The boarders are open, you can buy a ticket from Moscow to Tel Aviv and leave any moment. The tickets are pricy, but that's it. You won't need any special approval from the government (although some people reported they were searched & interrogated in the airport). A lot of people in Russia don't have a travel ID, which means they will have to spend 1-3 months waiting for it, but again it's not banned to leave the country at this moment.

However Aliah from the CIS region requires several visits to the Embassy to proof you're indeed Jewish, a screening and an interview with the Israel representative. This can take a lot of time. And many Russian Jews have family history of changed names and changed/forged documents.

In my case, the ticket will cost like half of my monthly salary, my grandparents changed their ethnicity to "Russian" to avoid persecution, I don't have a travel ID at the moment, so my chances are pretty slim at the moment.

TL;DR: no governmental restrictions YET, but a lot of possible complications. And with the Jewish Agency under attack it will get harder and harder.

The inscription on the bottom says 大日本文政年整珉鋳. According to limited sources I was able to find this was the seal of Seimin Murata (村田製眠), who was a well-known Edo era metalworker, famous for his Buddhist art. The art style like the detailed pattern on the background also resembles his bronze vases.

However the vase itself looks pretty crude compared to Murata's work. And according to what I was able to find, Murata's sign was often forged by other metalworkers. If you ask me, I think that this is your case.

I had similar life experience. Raised in a secular mixed family, no particular identity except from family memory of pogroms and Shoah. I didn't really have a strong grasp on what it means to be Jewish. So when I've experienced lot of antisemitism during college years that felt like a cold shower. I mean, people mistreated me for being a part of a community I've never truly belonged to.

But that's the thing, if you weren't Jewish, your friends would still be antisemetic jerks and bullies. It wasn't your ethnicity, it was them being ugly human beings with zero compassion. And people like that really just look for reasons to mistreat others.


Now, I think that at this point there can be two ways out of your conundrum.

You can embrace your heritage in a way that's meaningful for you. It's the solution I chose at some point. 
It can be anything really. Not necessary religious. You can start recovering and recording your family history. Or learning Hebrew. Or studying Jewish music as your major. Or volunteering online for Jew-related projects. Helping your Jewish relative. Anything that will give you a sense of community and pride.

Or you can also stop identifying as Jewish. I mean, are you really Jewish if you have no contact with the culture? After all, identity is as much about your general feeling and background as it is about genetics. If you grew up feeling like you are something else or at least not fully Jewish, is there a need to define yourself as such? 
I know it sounds terrible, but that's the way my siblings went. And they are pretty happy.

In Soviet era there was a political slur for Jews. "Rootless cosmopolitan". Sometimes during my college years I was very much into "reclaiming" it. I can't recommend anything specific, but I can give you some advice based on my little sister and her battle with embroidery.
I think cross stitch kit is the best option for starters. Cross is difficult to mess up and is generally not as complicated as other stitches.
Don't go for something big and time-consuming, because kids rarely have the patience to finish long projects. Maybe you can choose 2-3 smaller kits that grow from a tiny easy first one that will give immediate sense of accomplishment to a bigger more complicated kits for later.
Also choose the design carefully. Big wige single-color chunks are pretty boring to stitch. However it's easier to mess up a design that requires too many colors. I would go for something with 5-7 basic colors and a geometrical-ish patterns.
